This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which components (attention heads, FFNs) contribute to solving factual knowledge tasks, and how do these circuits for factual knowledge evolve over the course of model training?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge representation evolves during LLM pre-training, showing that models initially rely on general-purpose components which later specialize, with attention heads exhibiting high turnover and FFNs remaining more stable.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights into the hierarchical learning process of LLMs, where general components form first and later diversify, with attention heads being highly adaptive and FFNs providing stable processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads show high turnover and dynamic role transitions, while FFNs are more stable throughout training.
Location-based relations (LOC) converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations (NAME).
LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.
Answer-specific attention heads demonstrate the highest turnover, indicating frequent role changes.
FFNs act as a steady processing backbone, with most remaining in general roles.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level and the use of alternative interpretability techniques like activation patching across all snapshots.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based factual relations.
The analysis uses a fixed activation threshold for role classification, which may introduce bias.
Only a subset of training snapshots was analyzed, leaving gaps in tracking role transitions.
Direct comparison with other model families (e.g., Pythia) was not feasible due to architectural differences preventing the use of IFRs.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
Expand analysis to other domains, multilingual settings, and ambiguous queries.
Investigate the long-term impact of component dynamics on fine-tuning, pruning, and continual learning.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability.In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training.We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific and examine their stability and transitions.Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover.We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training.Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than namebased relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics.These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.We release the code and data. 1

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms cause LLMs to flip from correct to incorrect answers under re-evaluation, and how can we intervene to mitigate this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that cause unwanted uncertainty in LLMs and shows that targeted masking of these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without harming baseline accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Unwanted uncertainty in LLMs is not a byproduct of retrieval failure, but rather a consequence of specific attention heads that influence decision-making under re-evaluation; masking these heads can reduce flip behavior while preserving overall accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty.
A small set of non-retrieval attention heads disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts.
Masking these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection.
Masking uncertainty heads is effective only in cases of low uncertainty and can lead to overconfidence in incorrect answers in high-uncertainty tasks.
There exist some non-retrieval heads responsible for coherent outputs.
papers.limitation: Masking uncertainty heads can increase overconfidence in incorrect predictions in high-uncertainty tasks.
future_direction: Generalization to other models, architectures, and tasks.
Identifying and characterizing heads that yield incoherent outputs.
Better uncertainty head detection by analyzing attention head output vectors.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit unwanted uncertainty, a phenomenon where a model changes a previously correct answer into an incorrect one when re-prompted. This behavior undermines trust and poses serious risks in high-stakes domains. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms that drive this phenomenon. We adapt the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval framework and integrate a Flip-style re-evaluation prompt to simulate realistic answer-flipping scenarios. We find that retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty. Instead, we identify a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts. Masking these heads yields significant improvements, reducing flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection. However, when tested for downstream tasks, we observe trade-offs with flip behavior. Our findings contribute to the growing field of mechanistic interpretability and present a simple yet effective technique for mitigating uncertainty-driven failure modes in LLMs.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Are Pretrained Language Models Symbolic Reasoners over Knowledge?
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models learn factual knowledge? Specifically, can they perform symbolic reasoning to infer unseen facts, and what factors affect memorization of facts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that PLMs can learn some one-hop symbolic reasoning rules but overgeneralize, struggle with two-hop reasoning, and that memorization is influenced by frequency and schema conformity.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that BERT can to some extent infer facts not explicitly seen during training via symbolic rules, and effective knowledge acquisition combines memorization and symbolic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can learn one-hop rules like equivalence and implication, but overgeneralizes symmetry and inversion.
BERT struggles with two-hop reasoning (composition) unless provided with richer semantic context (schema).
BERT does not learn a general concept of negation; it relies on co-occurrences.
Memorization is successful for frequent facts and schema-conformant facts; exceptions are harder to memorize unless repeated.
When memory capacity is limited, schema-conformant facts and exceptions compete based on frequency.
papers.limitation:
Variation in generated data is more limited than in naturally occurring data.
Semantics are deliberately restricted to one rule only per generated corpus.
We do not investigate effects of model and corpus size.
future_direction: Relax the simplifying assumptions made in the study.
Improve PLMs' ability to learn symbolic rules by imposing additional inductive biases on architectures or modifying training corpora.
papers.abstract: How can pretrained language models (PLMs) learn factual knowledge from the training set? We investigate the two most important mechanisms: reasoning and memorization. Prior work has attempted to quantify the number of facts PLMs learn, but we present, using synthetic data, the first study that investigates the causal relation between facts present in training and facts learned by the PLM. For reasoning, we show that PLMs seem to learn to apply some symbolic reasoning rules correctly but struggle with others, including two-hop reasoning. Further analysis suggests that even the application of learned reasoning rules is flawed. For memorization, we identify schema conformity (facts systematically supported by other facts) and frequency as key factors for its success.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for knowledge storage in large language models, and how to distinguish between 'value neurons' that directly contribute to predictions and 'query neurons' that activate them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' in LLMs, and a method based on inner products to identify 'query neurons' that activate them, showing superior performance compared to other static methods.
papers.conclusion: The study proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate the 'query neurons' activating them, which aids in understanding the mechanism of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics tends to be stored in the same heads, while distinct semantics are stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
The proposed attribution method outperforms seven other static methods across three metrics.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B models; comparison across different models is needed.
Uses static methods for attribution and does not compare with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.
future_direction: Compare static methods with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.
Explore knowledge storage in other types of knowledge and across different models.
Improve attribution methods to better capture the importance of deepest layers and interpretability of query neurons.
papers.abstract: Identifying important neurons for final predictions is essential for understanding the mechanisms of large language models. Due to computational constraints, current attribution techniques struggle to operate at neuron level. In this paper, we propose a static method for pinpointing significant neurons. Compared to seven other methods, our approach demonstrates superior performance across three metrics. Additionally, since most static methods typically only identify "value neurons" directly contributing to the final prediction, we propose a method for identifying "query neurons" which activate these "value neurons". Finally, we apply our methods to analyze six types of knowledge across both attention and feed-forward network (FFN) layers. Our method and analysis are helpful for understanding the mechanisms of knowledge storage and set the stage for future research in knowledge editing. The code is available on https://github.com/zepingyu0512/neuron-attribution.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Fact Grounded Attention: Eliminating Hallucination in Large Language Models Through Attention Level Knowledge Integration
papers.research_question: How can hallucination in Large Language Models be eliminated by integrating external knowledge directly into the attention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fact Grounded Attention (FGA), a method that biases transformer attention scores with knowledge from an external database via a grounding matrix, a learned gate, and hard vocabulary constraints to improve factual accuracy.
papers.conclusion: FGA demonstrates that targeted architectural modifications combined with external knowledge sources can substantially improve factual reliability, offering a practical path toward more trustworthy language generation in knowledge-intensive domains.
papers.key_findings:
FGA achieves 87.1% accuracy in zero-shot mode and 99.7% with fine-tuning on a technical specifications dataset, compared to a 6.3% baseline.
The method enables sub-second knowledge updates without model retraining.
Ablation studies show all three components (grounding matrix, gate, constraints) are necessary for optimal performance.
The learned gate effectively discriminates between factual and non-factual contexts, preventing over-grounding.
FGA introduces minimal computational overhead (under 3% latency increase).
papers.limitation:
Requires structured facts; procedural knowledge, implicit reasoning, and subjective information remain challenging.
Current entity recognition is rule-based; neural entity linking could improve coverage and accuracy at increased computational cost.
Struggles with complex reasoning requiring multiple facts (multi-hop reasoning).
Deterministic guarantee applies only when specific conditions are satisfied (gate confidence threshold, correct entity linking, KB coverage, allowed token set).
future_direction: Explore hierarchical and compositional fact representations.
Improve entity linking with neural methods.
Develop compositional grounding mechanisms for multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: "The greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance, it is the illusion of knowledge." Large Language Models have conquered natural language but remain prisoners of their own probabilistic nature--confidently hallucinating facts they never truly knew. We present Fact Grounded Attention (FGA), a novel architectural modification that transforms unreliable language models into deterministic truth tellers by injecting verifiable knowledge directly into the attention mechanism. Unlike existing approaches that patch hallucinations after generation or prepend retrieved text, FGA intervenes at the mathematical heart of the transformer--the pre-softmax attention scores--creating a model that cannot hallucinate when facts exist in its knowledge base. Our experiments across 1,107 technical queries spanning smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles demonstrate a transformation from 6.3% accuracy in vanilla Llama 3.2 to 99.7% accuracy with FGA. More critically, knowledge updates occur in under one second without retraining, compared to hours for parameter editing approaches. FGA doesn't just reduce hallucination--it eliminates it entirely for verifiable facts, marking a fundamental shift from probabilistic approximation to deterministic precision in neural language generation.

papers.title: Disentangling Deception and Hallucination Failures in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs by separating knowledge existence from behavior expression?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs, and constructs a controlled environment for analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Representational separability analysis shows that knowledge existence is a dominant signal in distinguishing failure modes.
Sparse autoencoder reveals feature groupings associated with different behavioral cases, indicating a global split driven by knowledge existence.
Activation steering can induce bidirectional transitions between correct and deceptive behaviors, demonstrating causal control over behavior expression.
Hallucination cases are not reversible via activation steering, highlighting the distinction between knowledge absence and suppression.
Deception involves suppression of knowledge expression rather than knowledge removal, as verified through jailbreak probing.
papers.abstract: Failures in large language models (LLMs) are often analyzed from a behavioral perspective, where incorrect outputs in factual question answering are commonly associated with missing knowledge. In this work, focusing on entity-based factual queries, we suggest that such a view may conflate different failure mechanisms, and propose an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression. Under this formulation, hallucination and deception correspond to two qualitatively different failure modes that may appear similar at the output level but differ in their underlying mechanisms. To study this distinction, we construct a controlled environment for entity-centric factual questions in which knowledge is preserved while behavioral expression is selectively altered, enabling systematic analysis of four behavioral cases. We analyze these failure modes through representation separability, sparse interpretability, and inference-time activation steering.

papers.title: Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment
papers.research_question: What causes negative bias in large language models during binary decision tasks requiring complex reasoning, and how can it be corrected through attention head analysis and tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Negative Attention Score (NAS) to quantify negative bias in LLMs and proposes NASA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that corrects bias by aligning attention heads identified via NAS.
papers.conclusion: NASA effectively mitigates negative bias in LLMs for binary decision tasks and serves as a useful interpretability framework for analyzing attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit negative bias in binary decision tasks, showing high precision but low recall and higher confidence for negative responses.
NAS correlates with negative confidence and identifies query-agnostic negative attention heads across domains.
NASA reduces the precision-recall gap and improves F1 scores while preserving general reasoning abilities.
NASA enhances model calibration by aligning prediction confidence with accuracy.
Fine-tuning negative attention heads in order based on NAS is effective, whereas random tuning leads to suboptimal results.
papers.limitation:
Further research is needed to understand the causes and mechanisms behind negative biases in LLMs.
Fine-tuning attention heads individually may not be time-efficient; more efficient training methods could be explored.
future_direction: Explore more time-efficient training methods for tuning attention heads.
Investigate integrated research approaches connecting various elements of negative bias.
papers.abstract: A binary decision task, like yes-no questions or answer verification, reflects a significant real-world scenario such as where users look for confirmation about the correctness of their decisions on specific issues. In this work, we observe that language models exhibit a negative bias in the binary decisions of complex reasoning tasks. Based on our observations and the rationale about attention-based model dynamics, we propose a negative attention score (NAS) to systematically and quantitatively formulate negative bias. Based on NAS, we identify attention heads that attend to negative tokens provided in the instructions as answer candidate of binary decisions, regardless of the question in the prompt, and validate their association with the negative bias. Additionally, we propose the negative attention score alignment (NASA) method, which is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique to address the extracted negatively biased attention heads. Experimental results from various domains of reasoning tasks and large model search space demonstrate that NASA significantly reduces the gap between precision and recall caused by negative bias while preserving their generalization abilities.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models generalize to implications of facts they are finetuned on, and what mechanisms (extractive structures) enable this out-of-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the extractive structures framework to explain how language models generalize to implications of finetuned facts, and empirically validates two predictions of how these structures are learned: a data ordering effect and a weight grafting effect.
papers.conclusion: The extractive structures framework provides a mechanism for understanding out-of-context reasoning, and the empirical findings (data ordering and weight grafting) support the hypothesis that these structures are learned during pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extractive structures (informative, upstream, downstream components) are identified in the OLMo-7b model for two-hop reasoning tasks, with MLPs and attention heads playing specific roles.
Fact learning occurs in both early and late layers, with early layers enabling first-hop generalization and late layers enabling second-hop generalization.
A data ordering effect is observed: extractive structures are learned only if facts precede their implications during training.
Weight grafting (weight-space arithmetic) can transfer newly learned extractive structures to predict counterfactual implications.
Attention heads, not just MLPs, can store factual information as weight changes.
papers.limitation: The nature of an alternative mechanism hinted at in the data ordering experiments remains unclear, and the finetuning process's dependence on hyperparameters and the pretrained model is not fully characterized.
future_direction: Developing an underlying theory of generalization that captures the dynamical nature of optimization.
Applying the extractive structures framework more broadly to understand and ground out-of-context generalization beyond two-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) can generalize to implications of facts that they are finetuned on. For example, if finetuned on ``John Doe lives in Tokyo," LMs can correctly answer ``What language do the people in John Doe's city speak?'' with ``Japanese''. However, little is known about the mechanisms that enable this generalization or how they are learned during pretraining. We introduce extractive structures as a framework for describing how components in LMs (e.g., MLPs or attention heads) coordinate to enable this generalization. The structures consist of informative components that store training facts as weight changes, and upstream and downstream extractive components that query and process the stored information to produce the correct implication. We hypothesize that extractive structures are learned during pretraining when encountering implications of previously known facts. This yields two predictions: a data ordering effect where extractive structures can be learned only if facts precede their implications, and a weight grafting effect where extractive structures can be transferred to predict counterfactual implications. We empirically demonstrate these phenomena in the OLMo-7b, Llama 3-8b, Gemma 2-9b, and Qwen 2-7b models. Of independent interest, our results also indicate that fact learning can occur at both early and late layers, which lead to different forms of generalization.

papers.title: When Does Syntax Mediate Neural Language Model Performance? Evidence from Dropout Probes
papers.research_question: When do language models use syntactic information causally? How can we design probes to avoid false negatives due to redundant encodings of syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dropout probes, a new neural probing architecture that encourages probes to use all relevant representations of syntax in model embeddings, enabling better causal analysis and performance improvement via syntactic information injection.
papers.conclusion: Dropout probes are effective for causal analysis of language models and can be used to improve model performance by injecting syntactic information, but further work is needed to extend the approach.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode syntactic information redundantly in their embeddings.
Dropout probes reveal causal use of syntactic representations in QA models where prior methods did not.
Injecting syntactic information at test time can improve QA model performance on syntactically challenging tasks.
NLI models do not show causal use of syntax even with dropout probes.
Dropout probes can boost model performance without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation of models for many layers, multiple probes, and many counterfactuals is computationally challenging.
The transparency benefits require access to the internals of the pretrained model.
The technique is limited to diagnosis of existing models and does not train models to respond appropriately to interventions.
future_direction: Studying pretrained models beyond those considered in this work.
Further research into redundancy in embeddings.
More investigation into inserting symbolic knowledge into neural representations.
New methods for training models to respond appropriately to interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield "false negative" causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in Mamba
papers.research_question: Does factual recall in the Mamba state space model exhibit locality similar to the patterns observed in autoregressive transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: Despite architectural differences, Mamba exhibits similar localization patterns for factual recall as transformers, and many interpretability methods developed for transformers can be adapted to Mamba.
papers.conclusion: Many interpretability methods from transformers can be adapted to Mamba, and factual recall in Mamba shows similar localization patterns, indicating architectural similarities in how different models store and recall facts.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patching in Mamba reveals high causal effects at early-middle layers (subject last token) and later layers (prompt last token), similar to transformers.
ROME editing can successfully insert facts in Mamba by modifying projection matrices, with Wo being the most effective.
The linearity of relation decoding (LRE) in Mamba is similar to transformers, with some relations being more linearly decodable than others.
Adapted attention knockout experiments show that Mamba propagates relation information in early layers and subject information in middle layers, similar to information flow in transformers.
There is a separation of roles between early-mid and later layers in Mamba for factual recall, analogous to findings in transformers.
papers.limitation: Performing attention knockout in Mamba is challenging due to the Conv+SSM operation, making it difficult to block specific edges like in transformers.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms of factual recall in the Mamba state space model. Our work is inspired by previous findings in autoregressive transformer language models suggesting that their knowledge recall is localized to particular modules at specific token locations; we therefore ask whether factual recall in Mamba can be similarly localized. To investigate this, we conduct four lines of experiments on Mamba. First, we apply causal tracing or interchange interventions to localize key components inside Mamba that are responsible for recalling facts, revealing that specific components within middle layers show strong causal effects at the last token of the subject, while the causal effect of intervening on later layers is most pronounced at the last token of the prompt, matching previous findings on autoregressive transformers. Second, we show that rank-one model editing methods can successfully insert facts at specific locations, again resembling findings on transformer LMs. Third, we examine the linearity of Mamba's representations of factual relations. Finally we adapt attention-knockout techniques to Mamba in order to dissect information flow during factual recall. We compare Mamba directly to a similar-sized autoregressive transformer LM and conclude that despite significant differences in architectural approach, when it comes to factual recall, the two architectures share many similarities.

papers.title: Understanding Fact Recall in Language Models: Why Two-Stage Training Encourages Memorization but Mixed Training Teaches Knowledge
papers.research_question: Why does two-stage training encourage memorization while mixed training teaches knowledge, and how do shared parameters internally support fact recall in mixed training?
papers.core_contribution: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The paper introduces cross-task gradient trace to analyze these parameters.
papers.conclusion: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The cross-task gradient trace tool can be used to analyze such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training yields more shared parameters (those influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples) than two-stage training.
Shared parameters are concentrated in critical attention heads and are key to enabling fact recall in mixed-trained models.
Ablating shared parameters leads to a larger performance drop in mixed-trained models compared to two-stage trained models.
Mixed training achieves more parameter-efficient fact recall, requiring fewer parameters to recover performance.
Shared parameters in mixed training are more centralized and functionally important for generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether similar mechanisms emerge in other cross-task settings.
papers.abstract: Fact recall, the ability of language models (LMs) to retrieve specific factual knowledge, remains a challenging task despite their impressive general capabilities. Common training strategies often struggle to promote robust recall behavior with two-stage training, which first trains a model with fact-storing examples (e.g., factual statements) and then with fact-recalling examples (question-answer pairs), tending to encourage rote memorization rather than generalizable fact retrieval. In contrast, mixed training, which jointly uses both types of examples, has been empirically shown to improve the ability to recall facts, but the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how these training strategies affect how model parameters are shaped during training and how these differences relate to their ability to recall facts. We introduce cross-task gradient trace to identify shared parameters, those strongly influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples. Our analysis on synthetic fact recall datasets with the Llama-3.2B and Pythia-2.8B models reveals that mixed training encouraging a larger and more centralized set of shared parameters. These findings suggest that the emergence of parameters may play a key role in enabling LMs to generalize factual knowledge across task formulations.

papers.title: The Queen of England is not England's Queen: On the Lack of Factual Coherency in PLMs
papers.research_question: What is the coherency of factual knowledge in Pre-trained Language Models, and how does it vary with different prompts and evidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of coherency for factual knowledge in PLMs, demonstrates that PLMs have low coherency, and finds that including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
papers.conclusion: PLMs have poor coherency in factual knowledge, but evidence paragraphs help. Future work should focus on architectural, data, and interface improvements.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs have low coherency in factual knowledge.
Autoregressive PLMs perform worse than masked PLMs.
Optimized prompts do not improve coherency.
Including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
Coherency varies significantly with paraphrased prompts.
papers.limitation: For N-1 or N-M relations, it is difficult to exclude every possible answer, and only answers present in LAMA are excluded, which might negatively affect the results.
future_direction: Improve PLMs on architectural level.
Improve PLMs on data level.
Improve pre-training objectives and interface.
papers.abstract: Factual knowledge encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) enriches their representations and justifies their use as knowledge bases. Previous work has focused on probing PLMs for factual knowledge by measuring how often they can correctly predict an object entity given a subject and a relation, and improving fact retrieval by optimizing the prompts used for querying PLMs. In this work, we consider a complementary aspect, namely the coherency of factual knowledge in PLMs, i.e., how often can PLMs predict the subject entity given its initial prediction of the object entity. This goes beyond evaluating how much PLMs know, and focuses on the internal state of knowledge inside them. Our results indicate that PLMs have low coherency using manually written, optimized and paraphrased prompts, but including an evidence paragraph leads to substantial improvement. This shows that PLMs fail to model inverse relations and need further enhancements to be able to handle retrieving facts from their parameters in a coherent manner, and to be considered as knowledge bases.

papers.title: Dynamic Memory Inference Network for Natural Language Inference (2017)
papers.research_question: How can Dynamic Memory Networks be applied to improve performance in Natural Language Inference tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Dynamic Memory Networks are effective for Natural Language Inference by leveraging episodic memory updates and attention mechanisms, improving inference accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The Dynamic Memory Network framework effectively enhances Natural Language Inference by integrating episodic memory updates and attention mechanisms, offering a promising approach for future NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic Memory Networks with episodic memory updates improve accuracy in Natural Language Inference tasks.
Attention mechanisms in DMNs enable the model to focus on critical parts of sentences for better inference.
Multi-hop reasoning allows the model to revisit and refine memory states, mimicking human cognitive processes.
The proposed approach shows potential for complex NLI tasks but has computational limitations.
Experiments on SNLI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of DMNs over traditional encoding methods.
papers.limitation: Training DMNs is time-consuming and computationally expensive due to multiple memory hops and attention mechanisms.
future_direction: Reducing computational complexity and optimizing memory structures in DMNs.
Integrating advanced sentence encoders like transformers to capture long-distance dependencies.
Extending DMN framework to other NLP domains such as dialogue systems and question answering.
papers.abstract: In this paper, the NLI task is viewed as a question - and - answer problem, which leads to proposing the application of DMNs to enhance performance. NLI classifies the relationship between two sentences as entailment, contradiction, or neutral. It is necessary for many NLP applications, including question - answering, text summarization, and information retrieval. The most significant contribution of the paper is to demonstrate that DMNs are effective for episodic memory and experiment with DMNs outside of their original domain. This feature allows the model to incrementally update and reawaken memory, which provides a more nuanced view of the interactions of the sentences and hence also improves the accuracy of its inferential process. Furthermore, the paper analyses the aspects of the employed attention mechanisms in the structure of DMNs that enhance the capability of the model to pay attention to the essential words and phrases for successful task completion. The study highlights the impact of integrating the episodic memory updates with the attention mechanisms due to extensive experimentation, showing the benefits of such an NLI improvement and the potential for enhancing other NLP tasks.

papers.title: Do Language Models Understand Anything? On the Ability of LSTMs to Understand Negative Polarity Items
papers.research_question: Does an LSTM language model understand the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and can it detect the scope of the licensing context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that an LSTM language model can detect the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and that the model's hidden representations encode information about the scope of the licensing context.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM model is capable of handling NPI constructions and the licensing signal can be extracted from its hidden representations, paving the way for linking linguistic theory to neural models.
papers.key_findings:
The model assigns lower perplexity to sentences with correct NPI licensing compared to ungrammatical counterparts.
The model shows a strong preference for NPIs in negative contexts over positive contexts.
The model's hidden states can be used to predict the scope of the licensing context with high accuracy.
The model outperforms a baseline using GloVe embeddings in scope detection.
The effect of distance between NPI and licensing context: the model's performance degrades with longer distances.
papers.limitation:
The model's ability to handle NPI constructions degrades with longer distances between the NPI and the licensing context.
The study is limited to a subset of NPIs (those licensed by negative operators) and does not cover the full diversity of NPI constructions.
future_direction: Investigate a wider typological range of NPI constructions
Compare model performance with human judgments
Design entailment tasks based on linguistic hypotheses about NPI licensing
papers.abstract: In this paper, we attempt to link the inner workings of a neural language model to linguistic theory, focusing on a complex phenomenon well discussed in formal linguistics: (negative) polarity items. We briefly discuss the leading hypotheses about the licensing contexts that allow negative polarity items and evaluate to what extent a neural language model has the ability to correctly process a subset of such constructions. We show that the model finds a relation between the licensing context and the negative polarity item and appears to be aware of the scope of this context, which we extract from a parse tree of the sentence. With this research, we hope to pave the way for other studies linking formal linguistics to deep learning.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: In Praise of Stubbornness: An Empirical Case for Cognitive-Dissonance Aware Continual Update of Knowledge in LLMs
papers.research_question: What happens when LLMs encounter contradictory information, and can selective plasticity help maintain knowledge integrity?
papers.core_contribution: Contradictory updates in LLMs cause catastrophic interference on unrelated knowledge, while non-contradictory updates are safe. Selective plasticity helps for non-contradictory updates but fails for contradictory ones. Contradictions can be detected with high accuracy using model features.
papers.conclusion: LLMs lack a contradiction filter, leading to catastrophic interference from contradictory updates. This motivates new architectures that can resist contradictions, possibly by incorporating cognitive dissonance detection, append-only updates, and selective plasticity.
papers.key_findings:
Contradictory updates cause catastrophic interference, destroying up to 80% of unrelated knowledge even with few contradicting facts.
Non-contradictory updates can be integrated safely with minimal forgetting.
Selective plasticity (avoiding stubborn neurons) improves retention for non-contradictory updates but fails for contradictory updates.
Contradictory information can be detected with >95% accuracy using internal or output model features.
The catastrophic interference from contradictory updates persists across model scales (GPT-2 to GPT-J-6B) and training methods.
papers.limitation:
The use of simple factual statements may not capture complex knowledge conflicts.
Contradiction detection generalizability to nuanced scenarios is untested.
Scale limitations: small tracked knowledge relative to model capacity, and unclear effects in larger commercial models.
future_direction: Explore architectures that incorporate cognitive dissonance detection, append-only updates, and selective plasticity.
Design dedicated datasets and benchmarks for conflict detection.
papers.abstract: Through systematic empirical investigation, we uncover a fundamental and concerning property of Large Language Models: while they can safely learn facts that don't contradict their knowledge, attempting to update facts with contradictory information triggers catastrophic corruption of unrelated knowledge. Unlike humans, who naturally resist contradictory information, these models indiscriminately accept contradictions, leading to devastating interference, destroying up to 80% of unrelated knowledge even when learning as few as 10-100 contradicting facts. To understand whether this interference could be mitigated through selective plasticity, we experiment with targeted network updates, distinguishing between previously used (stubborn) and rarely used (plastic) neurons. We uncover another asymmetry: while sparing frequently-used neurons significantly improves retention of existing knowledge for non-contradictory updates (98% vs 93% with standard updates), contradictory updates trigger catastrophic interference regardless of targeting strategy. This effect which persists across tested model scales (GPT-2 to GPT-J-6B), suggests a fundamental limitation in how neural networks handle contradictions. Finally, we demonstrate that contradictory information can be reliably detected (95%+ accuracy) using simple model features, offering a potential protective mechanism. These findings motivate new architectures that can, like humans, naturally resist contradictions rather than allowing destructive overwrites.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations.
