Moreover, we highlight the risks of grounding faithfulness findings on out-of-distribution samples. In this work, we leverage a causal mediation technique called activation patching, to measure the faithfulness of an explanation towards supporting the explained answer. Our proposed metric, Causal Faithfulness quantifies the consistency of causal attributions between explanations and the corresponding model outputs as the indicator of faithfulness. We experimented across models varying from 2B to 27B parameters and found that models that underwent alignment tuning tend to produce more faithful and plausible explanations. We find that Causal Faithfulness is a promising improvement over existing faithfulness tests by taking into account the model's internal computations and avoiding out of distribution concerns that could otherwise undermine the validity of faithfulness assessments. We release the code in \url{https://github.com/wj210/Causal-Faithfulness}

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Hallucinate Less by Thinking More: Aspect-Based Causal Abstention for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we enable early abstention in Large Language Models by analyzing the internal diversity of their parametric knowledge through causal inference to prevent unreliable responses?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Aspect-Based Causal Abstention (ABCA), a framework that enables early abstention in LLMs by modeling knowledge heterogeneity through aspect-conditioned causal inference, improving abstention reliability and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: ABCA provides a causally principled framework for early abstention by probing diverse knowledge aspects, effectively reducing hallucinations and offering interpretable abstention decisions.
papers.key_findings:
ABCA achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple abstention benchmarks, outperforming existing post-hoc methods.
The framework distinguishes between knowledge conflict (Type-1) and knowledge insufficiency (Type-2) abstention, providing interpretable decisions.
ABCA improves answering accuracy on answerable questions while maintaining high abstention accuracy on unanswerable ones.
The dual-agent aspect discovery mechanism effectively identifies causally valid conditioning variables and aspects.
Case studies reveal limitations such as invalid aspect conditioning leading to incorrect abstention and aggregation on spurious facts despite consensus.
papers.limitation:
Invalid aspect conditioning (e.g., using a non-meaningful dimension like 'Number of') can lead to incorrect abstention decisions.
Strong agreement across discovered aspects may still lead to incorrect answers if the aspects overlook disambiguating information in the query.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce fluent but factually incorrect responses, a phenomenon known as hallucination. Abstention, where the model chooses not to answer and instead outputs phrases such as "I don't know", is a common safeguard. However, existing abstention methods typically rely on post-generation signals, such as generation variations or feedback, which limits their ability to prevent unreliable responses in advance. In this paper, we introduce Aspect-Based Causal Abstention (ABCA), a new framework that enables early abstention by analysing the internal diversity of LLM knowledge through causal inference. This diversity reflects the multifaceted nature of parametric knowledge acquired from various sources, representing diverse aspects such as disciplines, legal contexts, or temporal frames. ABCA estimates causal effects conditioned on these aspects to assess the reliability of knowledge relevant to a given query. Based on these estimates, we enable two types of abstention: Type-1, where aspect effects are inconsistent (knowledge conflict), and Type-2, where aspect effects consistently support abstention (knowledge insufficiency). Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ABCA improves abstention reliability, achieves state-of-the-art performance, and enhances the interpretability of abstention decisions.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: In Machina N400: Pinpointing Where a Causal Language Model Detects Semantic Violations
papers.research_question: At which computational depth does a transformer first register a semantic anomaly, and does this temporal pattern align with the timing of the human N400 response?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that semantic anomaly detection in the transformer model Phi-2 emerges in mid-to-late layers, with decoding accuracy peaking around layer 22, and reveals a biphasic representational geometry with initial expansion followed by compression, paralleling human N400 dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that both artificial and biological language systems may postpone semantic anomaly detection until sufficient context is integrated, with parallels to human N400 responses, though mechanisms may differ.
papers.key_findings:
Decoding accuracy for semantic violations peaks at layer 22 with AUC 0.723, and is significant only in layers 18-30.
Participation ratio analysis shows that violations initially increase dimensionality in early layers (1-6), then decrease below control levels after layer 12.
The late emergence of anomaly detection suggests semantic integration occurs after syntactic processing, similar to human language comprehension.
papers.limitation:
Results are from a single model (Phi-2) and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
Stimuli have fixed violation position, which could allow the model to exploit positional regularity.
Only participation ratio was used for geometry analysis; other measures might reveal additional structure.
Statistical robustness relies on five-fold cross-validation; larger corpora could improve generality.
Linear logistic regression was the primary probe; non-linear methods might provide further insights.
future_direction: Replicate analysis in larger autoregressive LMs and bidirectional encoders to test architecture generality.
Randomize violation position and introduce graded expectancy manipulations in stimuli.
Use complementary geometry metrics like intrinsic dimensionality or manifold capacity.
papers.abstract: How and where does a transformer notice that a sentence has gone semantically off the rails? To explore this question, we evaluated the causal language model (phi-2) using a carefully curated corpus, with sentences that concluded plausibly or implausibly. Our analysis focused on the hidden states sampled at each model layer. To investigate how violations are encoded, we utilized two complementary probes. First, we conducted a per-layer detection using a linear probe. Our findings revealed that a simple linear decoder struggled to distinguish between plausible and implausible endings in the lowest third of the model's layers. However, its accuracy sharply increased in the middle blocks, reaching a peak just before the top layers. Second, we examined the effective dimensionality of the encoded violation. Initially, the violation widens the representational subspace, followed by a collapse after a mid-stack bottleneck. This might indicate an exploratory phase that transitions into rapid consolidation. Taken together, these results contemplate the idea of alignment with classical psycholinguistic findings in human reading, where semantic anomalies are detected only after syntactic resolution, occurring later in the online processing sequence.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Trustworthy Reasoning: Evaluating and Enhancing Factual Accuracy in LLM Intermediate Thought Processes
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework addressing a critical vulnerability in Large Language Models (LLMs): the prevalence of factual inaccuracies within intermediate reasoning steps despite correct final answers. This phenomenon poses substantial risks in high-stakes domains including healthcare, legal analysis, and scientific research, where erroneous yet confidently presented reasoning can mislead users into dangerous decisions. Our framework integrates three core components: (1) a specialized fact-checking classifier trained on counterfactually augmented data to detect subtle factual inconsistencies within reasoning chains; (2) an enhanced Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reinforcement learning approach that balances factuality, coherence, and structural correctness through multi-dimensional rewards; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability method examining how factuality improvements manifest in model activations during reasoning processes. Extensive evaluation across multi state-of-the-art models reveals concerning patterns: even leading models like Claude-3.7 and GPT-o1 demonstrate reasoning factual accuracy of only 81.93% and 82.57% respectively. Our approach significantly enhances factual robustness (up to 49.90% improvement) while maintaining or improving performance on challenging benchmarks including Math-500, AIME-2024, and GPQA. Furthermore, our neural activation-level analysis provides actionable insights into how factual enhancements reshape reasoning trajectories within model architectures, establishing foundations for future training methodologies that explicitly target factual robustness through activation-guided optimization.

papers.title: Facts as Experts: Adaptable and Interpretable Neural Memory over Symbolic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we interface a neural language model with an interpretable symbolic memory to make knowledge accessible and modifiable without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural language model (Facts-as-Experts) with an explicit interface to a symbolic fact memory, enabling knowledge updates without retraining and improving performance on knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method for interfacing a neural language model with a symbolic memory, demonstrating improved QA performance and the ability to modify knowledge without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
FaE outperforms baseline models (FOFE, EmQL, EaE) on FreebaseQA and WebQuestionsSP QA datasets.
FaE can effectively answer questions using new facts injected into its memory at inference time without retraining.
FaE can update stale memories by overwriting facts, though performance decreases when new facts contradict pretraining data.
Removing overlapping entity pairs between pretraining/finetuning and test data reduces performance, indicating some memorization of paraphrases.
FaE shows a zero-shot capability, answering around a quarter of answerable questions without fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: Updating stale memories (where new facts contradict pretraining data) is more difficult and results in a performance drop, indicating the mixing between contextual representations and knowledge requires further research.
future_direction: Addressing the difficulty of updating stale memories and the problem of deleting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Massive language models are the core of modern NLP modeling and have been shown to encode impressive amounts of commonsense and factual information. However, that knowledge exists only within the latent parameters of the model, inaccessible to inspection and interpretation, and even worse, factual information memorized from the training corpora is likely to become stale as the world changes. Knowledge stored as parameters will also inevitably exhibit all of the biases inherent in the source materials. To address these problems, we develop a neural language model that includes an explicit interface between symbolically interpretable factual information and subsymbolic neural knowledge. We show that this model dramatically improves performance on two knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks. More interestingly, the model can be updated without re-training by manipulating its symbolic representations. In particular this model allows us to add new facts and overwrite existing ones in ways that are not possible for earlier models.

papers.title: Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch For LLMs? Better Factuality Can Lead to Worse Context-Faithfulness
papers.research_question: Does enhancing factuality in LLMs lead to a decline in context-faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Factuality enhancement methods can improve factuality but significantly undermine context-faithfulness in LLMs, causing overconfidence in parametric knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Factuality enhancement methods pose risks to context-faithfulness, and future research should balance both factual accuracy and context adherence.
papers.key_findings:
Factuality enhancement methods lead to a significant decline in context-faithfulness, with editing accuracy dropping by up to 60.3%.
The probability of new knowledge tokens decreases while parametric knowledge tokens increase after applying factuality enhancement.
Hidden states become more aligned with parametric outputs after context injection.
future_direction: Explore strategies to balance factuality and context-faithfulness in LLMs.
papers.abstract: As the modern tools of choice for text understanding and generation, large language models (LLMs) are expected to accurately output answers by leveraging the input context. This requires LLMs to possess both context-faithfulness and factual accuracy. Extensive efforts have been made to enable better outputs from LLMs by mitigating hallucinations through factuality enhancement methods. However, they also pose risks of hindering context-faithfulness, as factuality enhancement can lead LLMs to become overly confident in their parametric knowledge, causing them to overlook the relevant input context. In this work, we argue that current factuality enhancement methods can significantly undermine the context-faithfulness of LLMs. We first revisit the current factuality enhancement methods and evaluate their effectiveness in enhancing factual accuracy. Next, we evaluate their performance on knowledge editing tasks to assess the potential impact on context-faithfulness. The experimental results reveal that while these methods may yield inconsistent improvements in factual accuracy, they also cause a more severe decline in context-faithfulness, with the largest decrease reaching a striking 69.7\%. To explain these declines, we analyze the hidden states and logit distributions for the tokens representing new knowledge and parametric knowledge respectively, highlighting the limitations of current approaches. Our finding highlights the complex trade-offs inherent in enhancing LLMs. Therefore, we recommend that more research on LLMs' factuality enhancement make efforts to reduce the sacrifice of context-faithfulness.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: Cracking Factual Knowledge: A Comprehensive Analysis of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are degenerate knowledge neurons (DKNs) defined and acquired, and what is their relationship to the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive definition of degenerate knowledge neurons (DKNs) from structural and functional perspectives and introduces the Neurological Topology Clustering method for accurate DKN acquisition, demonstrating that DKNs are linked to the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive definition of DKNs and introduces the neurological topology clustering method for precise DKN acquisition, and through extensive experiments demonstrates the critical role of DKNs in the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of PLMs.
papers.key_findings:
DKNs identified by the Neurological Topology Clustering method exhibit strong degeneracy, meaning suppressing a subset of Base Degenerate Components (BDCs) does not significantly affect prediction probability, while suppressing all BDCs does.
DKNs help PLMs cope with input interference, indicating their contribution to model robustness.
DKNs have strong fact-checking ability, outperforming knowledge neurons and direct PLM-based fact-checking.
PLMs utilize DKNs to learn new knowledge, as parameter changes during fine-tuning highly overlap with DKNs.
Efficient fine-tuning by freezing all MLP neurons except DKNs enables PLMs to learn new knowledge while preserving old knowledge, highlighting DKNs' role in evolvability.
papers.limitation:
Limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7b models; validation on larger models is needed.
Confined to factual knowledge; applicability to other knowledge types is unknown.
Generalizability across different languages and cultural contexts is an open question due to the use of English datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Previous research suggests that factual knowledge is stored within multi-layer perceptron weights, and some storage units exhibit degeneracy, referred to as Degenerate Knowledge Neurons (DKNs). Despite the novelty and unique properties of this concept, it has not been rigorously defined or systematically studied. We first consider the connection weight patterns of MLP neurons and define DKNs from both structural and functional aspects. Based on this, we introduce the Neurological Topology Clustering method, which allows the formation of DKNs in any numbers and structures, leading to a more accurate DKN acquisition. Furthermore, inspired by cognitive science, we explore the relationship between DKNs and the robustness, evolvability, and complexity of LLMs. Our execution of 34 experiments under 6 settings demonstrates the connection between DKNs and these three properties. The code will be available soon.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Attention Sinks: A 'Catch, Tag, Release' Mechanism for Embeddings
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why attention sinks emerge in later tokens, whether they encode semantically meaningful information, how they differ between pretrained and reasoning models, and the impact of query-key normalization on attention sinks.
papers.core_contribution: This paper uncovers the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism in LLMs, where attention sinks catch tokens, tag them with semantically meaningful information, and release the tags into the residual stream for later use. The mechanism is prevalent across model families, more pronounced in reasoning models, and persists despite query-key normalization.
papers.conclusion: This work uncovers and formalizes the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism mediated by attention sinks, showing that sinks implement a functional tagging system that propagates semantically meaningful information across tokens, offering a foundation for deeper mechanistic investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sinks implement a 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, where sinks catch tokens, tag them with a common direction, and release the tags into the residual stream.
Tags encode semantically meaningful information, such as the truth value of statements, as shown by probing experiments.
Reasoning-distilled models exhibit the mechanism more strongly, with more attention sinks and higher variance explained by tags.
Attention sinks remain prevalent in models with query-key normalization, despite the normalization's intended effect.
The mechanism can emerge through training in a minimal theoretical model designed to solve a sequence averaging task.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical model does not prove the mechanism is necessary and may not reflect real-world complexity.
The threshold-based metric for identifying attention sinks may not capture all such tokens and lacks a principled method for setting the threshold.
The connection between the mechanism and reasoning is suggestive but not causally established.
future_direction: Deeper mechanistic investigations into token interactions and the role of implicit memory in transformers.
Establishing a causal link between the mechanism and reasoning.
Exploring practical applications such as steering activations for alignment and safety, and preserving the mechanism in model compression.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often concentrate their attention on a few specific tokens referred to as attention sinks. Common examples include the first token, a prompt-independent sink, and punctuation tokens, which are prompt-dependent. While the tokens causing the sinks often lack direct semantic meaning, the presence of the sinks is critical for model performance, particularly under model compression and KV-caching. Despite their ubiquity, the function, semantic role, and origin of attention sinks -- especially those beyond the first token -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation demonstrating that attention sinks: catch a sequence of tokens, tag them using a common direction in embedding space, and release them back into the residual stream, where tokens are later retrieved based on the tags they have acquired. Probing experiments reveal these tags carry semantically meaningful information, such as the truth of a statement. These findings extend to reasoning models, where the mechanism spans more heads and explains greater variance in embeddings, or recent models with query-key normalization, where sinks remain just as prevalent. To encourage future theoretical analysis, we introduce a minimal problem which can be solved through the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, and where it emerges through training.

papers.title: Are All Spurious Features in Natural Language Alike? An Analysis through a Causal Lens
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between different types of spurious features in natural language, specifically irrelevant features versus necessary features, and how does this affect model robustness and debiasing methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the distinction between irrelevant and necessary spurious features in natural language using causal models and probabilities of necessity and sufficiency, showing that this distinction explains results of debiasing methods and model robustness.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that high PN spurious features are common in NLP tasks and pose unique challenges for evaluation and learning robust models, unlike low PN features.
papers.key_findings:
High PN spurious features are necessary for prediction and interact with other features, unlike low PN features which are irrelevant.
Data balancing does not lead to invariant performance for high PN spurious features.
Removing high PN spurious features from representations using methods like INLP significantly hurts task performance.
High PN spurious features remain extractable from representations even after debiasing, whereas low PN features become less extractable.
Evaluation of robustness to high PN spurious features is challenging due to context dependence and the introduction of new features during perturbation.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on counterfactual quantities which are not observed and expensive to compute
Definitions do not directly tell us what training and evaluation methods are suitable for high PN spurious features
papers.abstract: The term `spurious correlations' has been used in NLP to informally denote any undesirable feature-label correlations. However, a correlation can be undesirable because (i) the feature is irrelevant to the label (e.g. punctuation in a review), or (ii) the feature's effect on the label depends on the context (e.g. negation words in a review), which is ubiquitous in language tasks. In case (i), we want the model to be invariant to the feature, which is neither necessary nor sufficient for prediction. But in case (ii), even an ideal model (e.g. humans) must rely on the feature, since it is necessary (but not sufficient) for prediction. Therefore, a more fine-grained treatment of spurious features is needed to specify the desired model behavior. We formalize this distinction using a causal model and probabilities of necessity and sufficiency, which delineates the causal relations between a feature and a label. We then show that this distinction helps explain results of existing debiasing methods on different spurious features, and demystifies surprising results such as the encoding of spurious features in model representations after debiasing.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Whether similar specialization for language emerges in large language models (LLMs) as in the human brain, and whether neuroscience-inspired localization methods can identify causally task-relevant units in LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs, demonstrating their causal role in language processing and their alignment with the human brain's language network.
papers.conclusion: Functional specialization for language exists in LLMs, with causally relevant units identifiable via neuroscience-inspired methods, showing parallels to the human brain. However, specialization for other cognitive functions like reasoning and social cognition is less consistent across models.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in all tested LLMs using a contrast between sentences and non-words, analogous to human neuroscience localizers.
Ablating a small fraction (e.g., 1%) of these language-selective units causes significant performance drops on language benchmarks, while ablating random units does not.
The response profiles of LLM language-selective units to various linguistic conditions (sentences, unconnected words, jabberwocky) qualitatively match those of the human language network.
Language-selective units show stronger alignment to brain activity in the human language network than randomly sampled units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for higher cognitive domains like reasoning (Multiple Demand) and social inference (Theory of Mind) is less consistent across models, with evidence found only in a subset.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units were evaluated using only one benchmark each (TOMi QA and MATH), not a comprehensive evaluation.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and constrained by traditional stimuli sets, which may limit investigation.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks for robustness and generalizability.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience constraints.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for the Multiple Demand and Theory of Mind networks beyond the top 1%.
papers.abstract: Badr AlKhamissi, Greta Tuckute, Antoine Bosselut, Martin Schrimpf. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Training-free Truthfulness Detection via Value Vectors in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do MLP modules in LLMs encode truthfulness-related statistical patterns, and can these patterns be leveraged for training-free truthfulness detection?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that certain value vectors within MLP modules exhibit consistent activation patterns correlated with content truthfulness, and introduces TruthV, a simple, interpretable, training-free method that leverages these patterns to detect truthfulness, outperforming existing baselines.
papers.conclusion: MLP modules contain interpretable statistical patterns that correlate with truthfulness and can be directly exploited for scalable, training-free truthfulness detection, providing new insights into LLM internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Certain value vectors in MLP modules show consistent argmax or argmin activation patterns when processing truthful versus untruthful content.
These truthfulness-related value vectors are predominantly located in the middle and final layers of the model.
The selected value vectors do not correspond to interpretable token-level concepts when projected into vocabulary space, suggesting they encode more abstract properties.
TruthV, which ensembles predictions from these value vectors, significantly outperforms NoVo and log-likelihood baselines on the NoVo benchmark.
Value vectors selected from one dataset show some generalization to others, but performance is best when selected from the target dataset.
papers.abstract: Large language models often generate factually incorrect outputs, motivating efforts to detect the truthfulness of their content. Most existing approaches rely on training probes over internal activations, but these methods suffer from scalability and generalization issues. A recent training-free method, NoVo, addresses this challenge by exploiting statistical patterns from the model itself. However, it focuses exclusively on attention mechanisms, potentially overlooking the MLP module-a core component of Transformer models known to support factual recall. In this paper, we show that certain value vectors within MLP modules exhibit truthfulness-related statistical patterns. Building on this insight, we propose TruthV, a simple and interpretable training-free method that detects content truthfulness by leveraging these value vectors. On the NoVo benchmark, TruthV significantly outperforms both NoVo and log-likelihood baselines, demonstrating that MLP modules-despite being neglected in prior training-free efforts-encode rich and useful signals for truthfulness detection. These findings offer new insights into how truthfulness is internally represented in LLMs and motivate further research on scalable and interpretable truthfulness detection.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Co-occurrence is not Factual Association in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do language models struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations? Is it because they learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We propose two strategies to improve learning of factual associations: using text with implicit associations and active forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Language models are biased to learn co-occurrence statistics, which hinders learning of generalizable factual knowledge. Using implicit association text and active forgetting can improve learning of factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
Co-occurrence statistics are easily learned from text with explicit co-occurrence, while factual associations are more easily learned from text with implicit association.
Knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics does not generalize well beyond simple QA, while factual associations generalize well to reasoning tasks.
Co-occurrence statistics and factual associations are parameterized in different layers: co-occurrence in middle layers, factual associations in lower layers.
Training on text with implicit association improves generalization of learned knowledge.
Active forgetting (resetting upper layer parameters) unblocks learning of factual associations and improves generalization.
papers.limitation:
Variation in forms of text: only two forms of text expressing factual knowledge are considered.
Methods for text generation: turning general text into text with implicit association may require complex rewriting.
The study is limited to finetuning of pretrained models, not pretraining from scratch.
Relationship to knowledge editing, knowledge-aware training and assisted reasoning: the study focuses on learning from raw text without annotations or reasoning assistance.
future_direction: Expand the investigation of knowledge learning efficiency to the pretraining phase.
Explore scalable data generation methods for efficient knowledge learning.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models can encode a large amount of knowledge and utilize it for various reasoning tasks, yet they can still struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations. In this work, we show that the reason for this deficiency is that language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We identify the differences between two forms of knowledge representation in language models: knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics is encoded in the middle layers of the transformer model and does not generalize well to reasoning scenarios beyond simple question answering, while true factual associations are encoded in the lower layers and can be freely utilized in various reasoning tasks. Based on these observations, we propose two strategies to improve the learning of factual associations in language models. We show that training on text with implicit rather than explicit factual associations can force the model to learn factual associations instead of co-occurrence statistics, significantly improving the generalization of newly learned knowledge. We also propose a simple training method to actively forget the learned co-occurrence statistics, which unblocks and enhances the learning of factual associations when training on plain narrative text. On both synthetic and real-world corpora, the two proposed strategies improve the generalization of the knowledge learned during finetuning to reasoning scenarios such as indirect and multi-hop question answering.

papers.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the faithfulness of natural language explanations that claim individual neurons in a language model represent a concept?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework with observational and intervention modes to evaluate natural language explanations of neurons, and applies it to show that GPT-4-generated explanations for GPT-2 XL neurons have low faithfulness and causal efficacy.
papers.conclusion: Natural language may not be the best medium for model explanations due to vagueness and ambiguity, and neurons may not be the optimal unit of analysis; structured formalisms and analysis of neuron groups are promising alternatives.
papers.key_findings:
Even among the top 0.6% of neurons with GPT-4 explanation scores ≥0.8, explanations achieve only 0.64 precision and 0.50 recall.
Intervention-based evaluation shows GPT-4 explanations have little to no causal efficacy, performing similarly to random baselines.
Individual neurons are not effective causal mediators; causal effects require aggregating over many neurons, especially in early MLP layers.
Natural language explanations are often vague and ambiguous, making them unreliable for technical decision-making.
The GPT-4 score used by Bills et al. (2023) is insensitive to Type I errors and does not guarantee faithful explanations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on GPT-2 XL; results may not extend directly to other architectures.
Faithful explanations could be used for malicious manipulations of models.
future_direction: Use structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages) instead of natural language for explanations.
Analyze groups of neurons or other network components (e.g., attention heads, residual streams) as units of analysis.
Conduct similar evaluations on other model architectures.
papers.abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.

papers.title: Reducing Bias in Sentiment Analysis Models Through Causal Mediation Analysis and Targeted Counterfactual Training
papers.research_question: How to reduce bias in sentiment analysis models by leveraging causal mediation analysis to identify biased components and applying targeted counterfactual training for de-biasing.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a bias reduction method for sentiment analysis models that uses causal mediation analysis to identify layers causally implicated in gender bias and then applies counterfactual training only to those targeted layers, achieving improved fairness without loss of accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully reduces gender bias in BERT sentiment models by using causal mediation analysis to target specific layers and then applying counterfactual training, resulting in improved fairness without compromising accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Causal mediation analysis can identify specific layers in BERT that contribute to gender bias.
Targeted counterfactual training on those identified layers reduces bias effectively.
The proposed method achieves higher fairness (lower Wasserstein distance) compared to baseline methods like full-model counterfactual training and dropout regularization.
The method maintains sentiment prediction accuracy while improving fairness, avoiding the accuracy-fairness trade-off.
The approach is validated on two sentiment analysis datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and evaluated on the Equity Evaluation Corpus (EEC).
papers.limitation: Limited to two datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and one fairness metric (p-Wasserstein).
future_direction: Apply the method to other biases on sensitive attributes such as ethnic groups, skin colour, and country.
Test the method on a broader range of datasets and with more fairness evaluation techniques.
Quantify the accuracy-fairness trade-off in real-world datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models provide high-accuracy solutions in many natural language processing tasks. In particular, they are used as word embeddings in sentiment analysis models. However, these models pick up on and amplify biases and social stereotypes in the data. Causality theory has recently driven the development of effective algorithms to evaluate and mitigate these biases. Causal mediation was used to detect biases, while counterfactual training was proposed to mitigate bias. In both cases, counterfactual sentences are created by changing an attribute, such as the gender of a noun, for which no change in the model output is expected. Biases are detected and eventually corrected each time the model behaviour differs between the original and the counterfactual sentence. We propose a new method for de-biasing sentiment analysis models that leverages the causal mediation analysis to identify the parts of the model primarily responsible for the bias and apply targeted counterfactual training for model de-biasing. We validated the methodology by fine-tuning the pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model for sentiment prediction. We trained two sentiment analysis models using the Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset and the Amazon Product Reviews, respectively, and we evaluated the fairness and prediction performances using the Equity Evaluation Corpus. We illustrated the causal patterns in the network and showed that our method achieves both high fairness and more accurate sentiment analysis than the state-of-the-art approach. Contrary to state-of-the-art models, we achieved a noticeable improvement in gender fairness without hindering sentiment prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: Interpreting Recurrent and Attention-Based Neural Models: a Case Study on Natural Language Inference
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the intermediate layers of neural models for natural language inference by visualizing the saliency of attention and LSTM gating signals?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces saliency-based visualization strategies for interpreting attention and LSTM gating signals in neural models for natural language inference, revealing insights not available from traditional methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization strategies effectively interpret neural models for NLI, offering new insights into model behavior and potential for improving models in future work.
papers.key_findings:
Attention saliency maps highlight which word alignments are critical for model decisions, unlike standard attention visualizations which may appear similar across different predictions.
Comparing models via attention saliency shows that ESIM-300 focuses on gender connections (e.g., 'John' vs 'man') while ESIM-50 does not, explaining performance differences.
LSTM gating signal saliency norms show that inference LSTM layers concentrate on key parts of sentences, whereas input LSTM layers have more spread-out saliency.
Saliency patterns for LSTM gates are consistent across different gates within the same layer, allowing joint interpretation.
The proposed visualization methods provide complementary understanding by revealing how models process information differently for contradiction, neutral, and entailment cases.
future_direction: Extend the study to other NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in natural language inference (NLI) tasks. While these models are widely explored, they are hard to interpret and it is often unclear how and why they actually work. In this paper, we take a step toward explaining such deep learning based models through a case study on a popular neural model for NLI. In particular, we propose to interpret the intermediate layers of NLI models by visualizing the saliency of attention and LSTM gating signals. We present several examples for which our methods are able to reveal interesting insights and identify the critical information contributing to the model decisions.
